script.opening_words: You're sitting at a kitchen table with a retirement statement in your hand, and the number on it says $44,000. You read it twice. Then you pick up your phone, and the first headline on the screen says, "The average American retirement account just hit an all-t
script.ending_words: at the real one, the one standing dead center in the line, has spent his entire working life comparing himself to a ghost and quietly concluding he was the one who came up short. You didn't come up short. You were handed the wrong number. Go get the right one.
script.analysis: Full 18265 canonical characters read. A persona-driven statistics explainer whose thesis is that headline "averages" (means) hide the median person: Desmond ($44,000 versus a $167,000 headline), Renata (buy-now-pay-later groceries) and Gerald (the orthodontist who inflates the mean). Structure: kitchen-table hook, mean-versus-median explanation, $400 emergency, cards, cars, BNPL, household debt, retirement and Social Security, "what it feels like", housing, steelman of improvement (401k default effect), subscriptions and lottery, Gerald reveal, held-back net-worth number, then three actions and a kitchen-table close. Strong throughline and an explicit open loop (the held-back worst number) that is paid off. Weaknesses: the opening example arithmetic is wrong ($1,045,000, not just under $1.5 million), the $770 a month figure matches annual not monthly deposits, the $427,000 median home price does not match the FRED series inspected, the 77% payable figure differs from secondary reports (78%), and most statistics (Vanguard, SHED, SCF, NY Fed breakdown, SS) are recall or secondary only. Mid-late mention of a school community. Persona stories are not data.
beat_map: Hook: kitchen table, $44,000 statement versus "record $167,000" headline; Desmond Ruiz, "the most statistically normal man in America".
Promise: both numbers true; "the man hiding inside that gap"; one worse number held to the end.
Mean versus median: nine at $50,000 plus one at $10 million; "the median is a person, the mean is a rumor".
The $400 emergency: 37% cannot cover; brake pads and water heater.
Credit cards: 22% rates, 2% minimum payment on $2,000, $160 billion annual interest.
Cars: $770 payment, 8% for 40 years to $2.4 million, 84-month loans, subprime delinquencies.
BNPL groceries and Renata; "arithmetic that stopped working".
Household debt $18.8 trillion composition; student-loan delinquency trapdoor.
Retirement: 4% rule on $44,115 gives $147 a month; Social Security reliance; one in five over 50 has nothing; trust fund late 2032; 401k hardship withdrawals.
What it feels like: cereal aisle, check-engine light, field trip, 2 a.m. arithmetic.
Housing: price-to-income about 5:1 versus 3.2 (1990) and 2.2 (1970); renters over 30% of income; first-time buyer age contested.
Steelman: 401k participation 86% because of auto-enrol (94% versus 64%), poverty down, low-wage real wages up.
Subscriptions $219 vs believed $86; lotteries $104.7 billion; financial literacy jab.
Gerald the orthodontist reveal: the mean is inflated; "you were measured with a ruler built crooked on purpose".
Payoff of the held number: median net worth $192,900 versus mean $1,063,700; $57,900 without home equity.
Actions: stop using the mean, change one default, automate, raise contribution 1%, take the $770 seriously; Desmond, Renata and Gerald close at the kitchen table.

claim_audit.stored_text_witness:

claim_audit.assessment: [INDEPENDENT_CALCULATION_VERIFIED] Contradicted by the script's own inputs: nine people at $50,000 plus one at $10 million average (450,000 + 10,000,000) / 10 = $1,045,000, not just under $1.5 million. When the 10th person leaves the average falls to $50,000, a drop of $995,000, not "about a million and a half". The mean-versus-median lesson is sound; the stated figures are wrong.

topic.analysis: Why headline average statistics about household finances (means) mislead, shown across emergency savings, debt, retirement, housing and net worth, with the median person as the real benchmark.
topic.audience_problem: Middle-income adults who feel behind after seeing average-wealth and average-retirement headlines.

topic.narrative_angle: The shocking statistic is that the average American does not exist.

topic.competition: Same-channel nearest-age peers in K01; not an independent niche or causal test
